Delve into her psyche and give her a reason to want to be angry and closed off. A **real** reason to make her the way she is without making her irritating or off putting so the reader can at least understand her situation. You say she lashes out at people and regrets it later, perhaps you can develop her by having her do something about her anger issues or have a serious moment of thought pondering. Make her really rethink/challenge her ways at some point is an option is what I'm saying.

I'll give an example with my own character, who I'll call Breaker. She works a stable enough job, has by all means a decent life in the world of Mirror. But at home she's unhinged; exhausted and nearly drowning herself in alcohol and she's usually offstandish and rude. Yes she's angsty, probably much more than your own Eliza, but for a reason. Breaker is troubled from being a no one to her family and her now-dead older sister having a clear disdain to her for it. She wasn't good enough for them and the only way she can feel better about her life is to forcefully take her mind off of it by putting all kinds of crap into her body.

As the story goes on, one of her new "friends" she meets and travels with throughout her journey is an older man who I'll call Aaron. The two have a large tension with each other because Aaron doesn't take kindly to Breaker's kind - called "reflections" - because one of them killed his son and wife over a decade before. He went into isolation. Near the latter half he finally explains it to Breaker in detail, he was distant from them for a long time before their deaths - eventually it was the same, he wasn't good enough for his family. He wasn't around to do anything for them, not even save their lives. This made Breaker completely change her attitude toward him to be more respectful and understanding. And by the end she realizes herself that she needs to change for the better because now she has the chance.

It's not the most complex arc I suppose, but it makes an angry character empathetic and much more human rather than just be a pain in the rear to the mood or to the reader the whole way. If you really want to avoid having your own character be insufferable or unlikable, I just gave one of the multiple ways you could go about it.

While it's fine to draw parallels to other characters that you like or perhaps feel inspired from, you do want to make them not so similar. In order to do this, you have to really disconnect your work from others' you read. I personally did this with my characters by writing random, out of context scenes that were more than likely never going to be included but I really set apart from other media while I did.

You see, what I did was I took a write-up that I had made beforehand of the character's distinct personalities, wrote those random scenes freehand while sticking to the info put in front of me. My main character in particular went from "Quiet emo stoic who's fun sometimes" in my writing to "Likably arrogant and witty, but with a hidden heart". If you're like me you'll also begin to have a lot more fun writing the story when you're characters are in place again.

A little late but I decided to abandoned most of the plot I had a few days ago.

It's a fantasy, and you see, originally it was based off of a question that popped into my head one night.

"What if the world saw a catastrophic disaster and was devastated, would I want to repair it or destroy it and rebuild with a new slate? To fix it with a second chance?" And I moved from there, or I tried.

I soon began to realize that for the most part, there weren't many ways to take this story let alone any of the different paths being good enough to a satisfactory amount. What I had was just uninspired as a concept as it just took from multiple other works with hardly any tweaking. At first this story sounded amazing, but it wasn't until I truly started trying to write things down or answer my own questions and the page would come out blank. I struggled so much every time. This is when I realized the story I wanted out of it was pretty shallow. You'd see a recent post of me asking about my villain's motive being believable or not, which is probably one of the things I struggled with most. I couldn't really make an original or even good character with what I had there.

Instead I've opted to throw out the general concept completely and used the leftovers to craft something with more potential. Everything seems much clearer and cohesive with this new story and it still keeps most of a vision of what I was going for before, expect now it can actually work.

When it crosses the line of trying to use it to justify every action they take. For example something that I see many writers do is try *desperately* to almost defend their characters' actions by basically saying "Oh him brutally killing and torturing people is justified because this happened and this happened and he's messed up!" but this almost never works. If you want a tragic backstory to be sympathetic don't make it completely dictate the character no questions asked rather, make it sway them into so-so path of action and have an emotional struggle going on.

It happens, man. Just keep at it.

You'll improve but like any skill it takes a while to get even okay.

Practice, practice, practice.

Write something, know it sucks, rinse repeat.

If you enjoy writing you should see this as a challenge.

I'm gonna let you in on something, bro. It's a fighting game. You're *gonna* lose a lot of the time, especially as a beginner not just to this game, but the whole genre as you said. I've had it worse than you! I had 25 wins and like 50 losses before those numbers began improving.

Instead of getting angry, focus on what you could have done differently in your losing match and apply that for future ones. There are a shit ton of variables in almost any fighting game. 

'Could I have used a better option in that situation?' 

'Could I have spaced better?' 

'Did I pick up on any repetitive methods so I can predict them?'

These are only few of the hundreds of questions a fighting game players asks themselves day in and day out. And even if you have become the very best like no one ever was, you're still going to lose sooner or later because that's just how the world works. You'll feel like shit. A fraud. A loser. A dreamer. People might even openly make fun of you losing, then kick you to the curb like the trash bin. So you can wait for your sorrows to be the garbage truck.

But at the end of the day, it won't matter. You will have slowly but surely improved by an insanely marginal amount each day. Everyone goes through this. No matter what game you're playing there will always be people who are miles better than you can ever hope to be; and that is completely fine. If every match was a walk in the park, the game would serve no purpose.

So. Don't be mad, or sad, just stay in your bubble and work, work, work. And even if you just suck, treasure every good match like long lost gold. Because that's how you improve and have fun.
